name: Adjust The Presentation (Hard Version)
description: This is the hard version of the problem. In the two versions, the constraints on $$$q$$$ and the time limit are different. In this version, $$$0 \leq q \leq 2 \cdot 10^5$$$. You can make hacks only if all the versions of the problem are solved. A team consisting of $$$n$$$ members, numbered from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$, is set to present a slide show at a large meeting. The slide show contains $$$m$$$ slides. There is an array $$$a$$$ of length $$$n$$$. Initially, the members are standing in a line in the order of $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ from front to back. The slide show will be presented in order from slide $$$1$$$ to slide $$$m$$$. Each section will be presented by the member at the front of the line. After each slide is presented, you can move the member at the front of the line to any position in the lineup (without changing the order of the rest of the members). For example, suppose the line of members is $$$[\color{red}{3},1,2,4]$$$. After member $$$3$$$ presents the current slide, you can change the line of members into either $$$[\color{red}{3},1,2,4]$$$, $$$[1,\color{red}{3},2,4]$$$, $$$[1,2,\color{red}{3},4]$$$ or $$$[1,2,4,\color{red}{3}]$$$. There is also an array $$$b$$$ of length $$$m$$$. The slide show is considered good if it is possible to make member $$$b_i$$$ present slide $$$i$$$ for all $$$i$$$ from $$$1$$$ to $$$m$$$ under these constraints. However, your annoying boss wants to make $$$q$$$ updates to the array $$$b$$$. In the $$$i$$$-th update, he will choose a slide $$$s_i$$$ and a member $$$t_i$$$ and set $$$b_{s_i} := t_i$$$. Note that these updates are persistent , that is changes made to the array $$$b$$$ will apply when processing future updates. For each of the $$$q+1$$$ states of array $$$b$$$, the initial state and after each of the $$$q$$$ updates, determine if the slideshow is good.
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10^4$$$). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains three integers $$$n$$$, $$$m$$$ and $$$q$$$ ($$$1 \le n, m \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$; $$$0 \leq q \leq 2 \cdot 10^5$$$) — the number of members and the number of sections. The second line of each test case contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n$$$ ($$$1 \le a_i \le n$$$) — the initial order of the members from front to back. It is guaranteed that each integer from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$ appears exactly once in $$$a$$$. The third line of each test case contains $$$m$$$ integers $$$b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_m$$$ ($$$1 \le b_i \le n$$$) — the members who should present each section. Each of the next $$$q$$$ lines contains two integers $$$s_i$$$ and $$$t_i$$$ ($$$1 \le s_i \le m$$$, $$$1 \le t_i \le n$$$) — parameters of an update. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$, the sum of $$$m$$$ and the sum of $$$q$$$ over all test cases do not exceed $$$2 \cdot 10^5$$$ respectively.
output_specification: For each test case, output $$$q+1$$$ lines corresponding to the $$$q+1$$$ states of the array $$$b$$$. Output " YA " if the slide show is good, and " TIDAK " otherwise. You can output the answer in any case (upper or lower). For example, the strings " yA ", " Ya ", " ya ", and " YA " will be recognized as positive responses.

approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 2021C2 — Adjust The Presentation (Hard Version) [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
